note_tweet.text:
How to choose between Muse and Grok Bot

The least useful agent comparison copies two feature lists and declares a winner. In practice, a disconnected tool, an unusable deliverable, or an unexpected action can matter more than the length of either list.

My recommendation is a testing order: start with Meta Muse for personal administration and goals; evaluate Grok Bot first for named responsibilities, recurring deliverables, and work across tools. Their capabilities overlap. This is a reading of official materials checked on October 28, 2026, not a head-to-head performance result.

Start with how the work is organized

Meta introduced Muse on September 8 and announced its Japan launch on October 23. These are existing developments, not news breaking today. Its positioning centers on a person’s goals, schedule, and everyday administration. [1] [2]

Grok Bot emphasizes named Bots with defined jobs and durable working context. Its skills describe how work is done; routines determine when it runs. [3] [4] That makes it worth testing first when you want an ongoing industry researcher and a separate editorial responsibility.

This is a preference, not a capability wall. Muse’s design article also describes a terminal, document and webpage creation, and continuing background work. [5] It is not limited to personal errands. Compare how much explanation and correction each product needs for your recurring tasks.

Check eligibility before designing the workflow. A regional Muse announcement does not establish worldwide access. Grok Bot’s current documentation lists compatible Cursor and SuperGrok subscriptions, among others; an X badge alone is not sufficient evidence of access. [2] [3] Verify the actual plan, limits, and connections available to your account.

The overlooked distinction is the permission boundary

Grok Bot’s detailed documentation says that Bots on the same account share a cloud computer, including files, browser sessions, and command-line credentials. Separate screens are not separate security boundaries. [6] Naming three Bots Researcher, Finance Assistant, and Personal Assistant does not automatically isolate their data.

Sharing makes handoffs easier: another Bot can continue saved work. It also changes what belongs in that environment. If clients or data classifications require strict separation, role descriptions are insufficient. Verify the product’s account or organizational isolation options; do not connect the data if those controls fail your requirements.

Muse’s security article describes separating the agent runtime from sensitive services, with an independent Sentinel controlling connector actions and network egress. [7] That is a vendor-disclosed architecture, not my security audit or proof of zero risk. Neither product’s documentation establishes that the other is necessarily unsafe.

Test a complete workflow

Consider a weekly technology brief. My proposed workflow is to collect specified sources with event dates, shortlist three candidates, prepare bilingual copy and illustrations, verify facts and calculations, and check that delivered files open. Stop at a reviewable draft. Missing sources should produce a gap report, not recycled figures presented as current.

In Grok Bot, start with one Bot completing the whole task before splitting research and editing. Its documentation recommends validating a one-time task before saving a skill and scheduling a routine. [4] Adding Bots too early may add handoff and debugging costs. Apply identical acceptance criteria to Muse; a terminal and file-generation capability do not establish delivery quality.

Define authorization separately for sending, purchasing, and publishing. Grok Bot documents approvals and Auto Review rules: Ask first takes precedence when it also matches an Allow automatically rule. Muse describes confirmation for consequential actions too. [1] [8] The account, recipient, and exact version must be identifiable. Website operation does not establish permission for every platform automation. Validate drafting and publishing separately.

The revealing cases are an expired login, an inaccessible source, or a damaged attachment. Does it stop and explain, or claim completion? Can it resume from a checkpoint without repeating an external action? Include those cases rather than judging only a smooth demonstration.

Price your review time as well as the subscription

Take a hypothetical example unrelated to either product’s actual plans. Suppose one option costs an extra $20 per month but saves two human minutes per accepted task. At $30 per hour, that releases $1 of time value per task. Twenty tasks cover the extra fee; 10 release $10 and 50 release $50.

The break-even assumes no additional setup or recovery cost. Extra costs raise the required volume. Released time is not necessarily cash savings: it matters only if time is actually freed and the opportunity-cost assumption is meaningful. Free entry does not mean zero total cost, and a higher fee does not establish better capability.

I would test the same 10 tasks on both products, repeating each batch twice: five sourced research summaries, three content deliverables, and two spreadsheet outputs. Keep sources, acceptance criteria, and budgets equal. Add expired-login and missing-source tests. If a product cannot deliver an item, record that instead of quietly substituting an easier task.

Track acceptable deliverables, human review minutes per task, serious errors, recovery outcomes, and total costs. Include failed attempts and rework. Ten tasks are a starting point, not proof of general reliability. The goal is to choose for your work, not crown a universal winner.

My decision

For personal preferences and life administration, I would start with Muse. For recurring research, file delivery, and explicit responsibilities, I would evaluate Grok Bot first. That preference follows their product organization, not a ranking of model intelligence.

If the necessary connection, regional access, subscription, or data separation is missing, postpone the migration. Watch recovery, visible permissions, accepted-delivery rate, and review effort—not only new model names. Keep the product that reduces repeated explanation and rework on your tasks.

note_tweet.text:
Muse和Grok Bot怎么选

选AI代理，我最怕看到一种比较：把功能列表抄一遍，最后宣布某款“全面碾压”。真到自己用，最耗时间的往往是接不上工具、结果要重做，以及不知道它下一步会动什么。

我的选择建议是：生活事务和个人目标管理，先试Meta Muse；有明确岗位、重复交付和跨工具协作的工作，优先评估Grok Bot。两者能力有重叠，这只是依据截至2026年10月28日官方资料提出的试用顺序，不是实测胜负。

先看任务怎样组织

Muse于9月8日发布，Meta在10月23日宣布它进入日本市场。这些是已有进展，不能当作今天刚发生。Meta把它定位为个人代理，围绕人的目标、日程和日常事务组织工作。[1][2]

Grok Bot则突出有名字、有职责、能长期保留工作上下文的Bots，以及skills和routines：前者保存做法，后者决定何时运行。[3][4] 因此，如果你需要“一个研究员长期盯行业，一个编辑整理稿件”，这种岗位式组织值得先试。

但别把这画成硬边界。Muse官方设计文章也明确写到终端、生成文档与网页、持续处理任务；它不是只能订餐的生活小助手。[5] 真正要比较的是：哪款能用更少的交代和纠错，完成你反复要做的事。

开通资格也要先过关。Muse的地区公告不能推导为全球开放；Grok Bot现行文档列出兼容的Cursor、SuperGrok等套餐，不能仅凭一个X蓝标推定已经能用。[2][3] 价格、额度、连接器以自己的实际入口核对。

最容易漏看的区别是权限边界

Grok Bot的详细文档写得很具体：同一账号下的Bots共享云电脑，文件、浏览器登录会话和命令行凭据也共享；每个Bot有自己的屏幕，不代表各自有独立的安全边界。[6] 研究员、财务助理、私人助理取三个名字，并没有自动把资料隔开。

这带来方便：一个Bot保存的工作，另一个可以接手。代价是你要先判断，共享环境里能否放这些资料。需要不同客户、不同保密等级的数据严格隔离时，不能靠角色说明解决，应核对产品实际的账号或组织隔离方案；不满足就不接入。

Muse的安全文章描述另一组控制：代理运行环境与安全敏感服务分开，连接器动作和网络出口由独立的Sentinel管理。[7] 这是厂商披露的架构，不是我做过的安全审计，也不构成“零风险”证明。两家的材料都不能用来推出“另一个一定不安全”。

拿一条真实工作流试而不是聊两句

假设每周要交一份科技选题简报。我的建议流程是：收集指定来源，记录事件日期和出处；筛选三个候选；按固定格式形成双语稿与配图；核对事实、数字和可打开的交付文件；最后停在待审状态。缺资料就报告缺口，不能拿旧数据补位。

在Grok Bot里，可以先让一个Bot完整跑通一次，再考虑分出研究与编辑职责。官方文档也建议先验证一次性任务，再保存为skill、安排routine。[4] 过早加很多Bot，可能只是增加交接和排错成本。Muse也应接受同样的交付验收，而不是因为有文件或终端能力就默认能做好。

发送、购买、发布必须单独定义授权边界。Grok Bot有审批和Auto Review规则，Ask first与Allow automatically同时命中时，前者优先；Muse也说明重要动作会请求确认。[1][8] 具体用什么账号、向谁发、发哪个版本，都要可辨认。能操作网站不等于所有平台都允许相应自动化，选题出稿与实际发布要分别验证。

真正看差距的时刻，是登录失效、来源不可读、附件损坏以后：它会暂停说明，还是编一个“已完成”？它能保留检查点继续，还是重新跑一遍造成重复动作？这些要列进试用题，不能只看顺畅的演示。

订阅费之外还有你的复核时间

做一个不对应任何真实套餐的假设算例：某方案每月多花20美元，但每件合格任务少用2分钟人工。若人工时间按30美元/小时计，每件释放1美元的时间价值，每月20件才覆盖这20美元；10件只有10美元，50件则是50美元。

这个临界点假设额外设置、失败恢复等成本差为零。若多出这些成本，所需任务数还会增加。节省的时间也不等于现金马上回到银行卡；只有时间确实被释放、且你认可这个机会成本，才有讨论价值。不要把免费入口当作零成本，也不要把贵当作能力证明。

我会拿同一批10件任务试两款，各重复两轮：5件有出处的研究摘要、3件按要求成稿的内容、2件表格交付。使用相同资料、验收标准和预算，另外安排登录失效与来源缺失的测试。某项无法交付，就如实记下，不悄悄换成容易任务。

记录合格交付数、每件人工复核分钟数、重大错误、恢复是否成功及总成本。失败和返工的开销也要算进去。10件只是起点，不足以证明整体可靠性；它的作用是让你看清自己的工作，而不是替全世界选冠军。

我的选择结论

如果主要想有人记住个人偏好、跟进生活安排，我会从Muse开始试；如果主要是周期性研究、文件交付和明确分工，我会先评估Grok Bot。这个倾向来自产品组织方式，不是对模型智力的排名。

如果核心工具连接不上、地区或套餐不支持，或者数据隔离不满足要求，就先不迁移。下一步观察的也不应只是新模型名字，而是接管恢复、权限可见性、交付成功率和真实复核负担。谁能在你的任务上省掉反复交代和返工，谁才值得留下。

[3] Grok Bot Docs  Overview https://t.co/6omTXiaBuu

State of the Personal Agents Ecosystem: October 27th, 2026

(Going to go from 5th place to 1st place 🥇)

5) Dots 

Lots of potential. Voice mode is very good. But VERY early, lacks tons of features, and is more of a research preview with a couple of features, than a real competitor atm.  Never count out @OpenAI though

Hero Mode: Voice mode with great orchestration.

Weaknesses: Expensive and missing tons of features

4) @instinct 

Honestly, the people that I know that are using Instinct, love Instinct. The harness is very good. it's proactive, and does a great job personalizing its responses to the user.

Hero Mode: Multiplayer. One of the few personal agent platforms that offers a true multiplayer experience (e.g. invite instinct into a group chat with your wife, etc)

Weakness: the very thing that makes it great, being served in text messages, and not within an app that offers features like artifacts, etc.

3) Claude #duet 

My sweet Duet. It's fast, its responsive, and proactive. You can feel the power with 5.5 as the backbone, but it's oh so early. Kind of feels like a talented 8th grader playing on the varsity team. 

Hero mode: Is very fast! Often it will find to-dos / follow ups within a minute of getting those alerts in slack + calendar.

Weakness: UX is confusing (when do you use channels vs groups) and features are very limited (no VM control, no secure password store, etc)

2) @Meta  @Muse 

My handsome, Carl. He's a good boy, and he tries really hard. He's just not that smart yet! He's proactive, affordable, has a great UX, and their voice mode actually slaps.

Hero Mode: built in artifacts within the app. I pretty much have my agent build me any kind of app I want to use. Also, access to their SDK!

Weakness: It's model (Spark + wonder) is generally slow, doesn't multitask well, wouldn't trust with coding, and is not SOTA. If it used Opus 5.5, it'd be the #1 option...

1) @bot 

Try and dethrone the king, I dare you. Grok bot is a beautiful blend of power, speed, and versatility. The damn thing just works. 

It uses the best model for the task (others should take note), has fantastic integration into the ecosystem, has the best VM experience out of all, templates are actually awesome, and if you're a coder, that's awesome too with its cursor integration.

Honestly, it's just a bit expensive. But if it's your daily driver at work,  like it is for most people that I know, then it's well worth the cost.

Hero Mode: SOTA models, Voice mode & a world class VM experience. 

Weakness: no built in artifacts. They recently launched pages, but that's lame. Let me build my own apps directly within the app to use like Muse.

--

Honestly though, they're all good. My advice to you: pick one, and go all in on it. Then once good with that one, find another one that would be good for another area of your life, and go all in on that.

Here is my current breakdown:

Muse: my personal agent helping me manage my life 

Grokbot: my work agent, helping me with routine tasks, and constant cloud based work

Duet: my super human agent to help me be the best employee I can be. With its quick speed, deep ecosystem support, and opus 5.5m it does really well with my connected tools helping me stay on top of everything.

--

What a time to be alive! Have fun and go explore =)

note_tweet.text:
Everyone's launching a personal AI agent.

Meta Muse. Grok Bot. Instinct. ChatGPT Dots. Hark. And now Claude Duet.

Here's what one actually is, explained simply.

A personal agent is an assistant with its own computer, your logins, and permission to come to you first instead of waiting for you to type.

That's the whole definition.

Under the marketing, every one is built from the same 7 parts:

1. Channel. Where it reaches you. Instinct lives in iMessage and WhatsApp. Duet is its own app.
2. Orchestration. How it splits up your requests. Grok Bot runs a team of named bots with a chief of staff on top.
3. Memory. What it knows about you. Muse keeps it in one editable file it calls your soul.
4. Computer. Where the work runs. All of them have a cloud browser, so they keep going with your laptop closed.
5. Hands. What it can touch. Muse and Instinct can phone a business for you.
6. Proactivity. When it decides to bother you. Even 5 check-ins a day starts to feel like spam.
7. Approval. Where you say yes. A chat bubble in Instinct. A screen inside an app in Duet, Grok Bot and Dots.

Why is every company building one?

Nobody's loyal to a model anymore. Grok Bot already runs Claude Opus 5.5 for some tasks.

The model is the engine. The agent is the interface you live with.

Whoever owns the moment you say yes owns the daily habit.

The personal agent race is the real race. Not the model race.

My pick for each job, with every prompt I'm running 👇
